analysis.one_liner: Lets unions require workers to join and pay dues as a job condition, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2023 with 26 cosponsors, all Democrats, sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would delete the section of federal labor law that lets states pass "right-to-work" laws, which make it illegal for a union contract to require workers to join the union or pay dues as a condition of their job. The bill would not itself create union security agreements; it would take away states' power to ban them, leaving unions and employers free to negotiate such clauses anywhere in the country. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, union members and workers in the roughly 26 right-to-work states would have gained the most: unions could negotiate contracts requiring dues payments from everyone they represent, giving unions more revenue and members, which historically supports higher negotiated wages and stronger grievance representation for all workers in a bargaining unit.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states pass right-to-work laws barring union-security agreements.

With 14(b) gone, labor contracts nationwide could require workers who benefit from union representation to pay dues or fees, ending the free-rider problem in which nonmembers get union-won wages and grievance representation without paying.
Stronger union finances and membership in the roughly 26 right-to-work states would, supporters argue, raise pay and bargaining power for workers there.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who prefer not to fund a union would have to pay dues or fees to keep their jobs; employers, especially in right-to-work states, would face higher labor costs and less flexibility in union agreements.

drawbacks.text: The bill would require workers who do not want to join a union to pay union dues or fees anyway, as a condition of keeping their job, in every state.
Employers, especially in the 26 right-to-work states, would face higher labor costs, and critics of mandatory-fee agreements argue this can reduce hiring and business expansion in those states.

The bill repeals state law authority wholesale rather than offering a middle path (such as requiring fee payments without full membership), giving no accommodation to states that have chosen the right-to-work policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is substantial for workers: closed-shop authority has historically been linked to higher wages and stronger union finances, and it ends the free-rider problem in the 26 right-to-work states. The costs and objections are real: workers who prefer not to fund a union would be required to pay as a condition of keeping their job, and businesses in formerly right-to-work states would face higher labor costs, which some economists argue can slow hiring. The bill also takes a blunt approach — a full repeal rather than a compromise such as allowing fee payments without full membership — and it was introduced with no path to enactment in a divided Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never took it up and Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on September 5, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It drew 26 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, in a chamber where Republicans held a narrow majority.
The bill's only recorded action was the referral; no subcommittee or full committee action, no markup, and no floor vote followed before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in right-to-work states are better off, since they continue to operate under laws that bar mandatory union-fee agreements; no worker's obligations changed.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the state right-to-work provision of federal labor law.

for.name: 26 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: House cosponsors, including Boyle, Kildee, Jayapal, McGovern, and Nadler
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 26 were Democrats.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before Congress ended.

against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda and committee chairs in the 118th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and the Republican House majority that controlled the committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's central effect is to let unions require dues-paying membership as a condition of employment in every state, reversing the right-to-work laws that 26 states have enacted. That would materially increase union membership rolls and revenue.
Businesses in right-to-work states would face mandatory union-fee arrangements they are currently spared, raising labor costs. Some would gain labor-peace stability; many would see costs rise.
